explanation: A grave accent slopes the other way, as in 'à la carte'. The hook under the c of 'façade' is a cedilla, from Spanish for 'little z'.

claims.text: The mark over the e in 'café' is an acute accent.
The mark in 'café' is not a grave accent, a circumflex or an umlaut.
A grave accent slopes the opposite way to an acute accent, and the a of 'à la carte' carries a grave accent.
The mark under the c of 'façade' is a cedilla.
The word cedilla comes from Spanish cedilla (zedilla), a diminutive of the name of the letter z, so it means 'little z'.

writerNotes: Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE 9.3). lint: content:check run on the batch until clean. claims: 5 listed, all high: the cedilla etymology (etymology) and c1 to c4 at the C26 quotation floor, though they are typographic facts anyone can see. datasets: none covers diacritics. One WebSearch, 'cedilla etymology Spanish zedilla diminutive of zeda letter z': Etymonline (English since the 1590s, from Spanish cedilla, zedilla, literally 'little z'), Merriam-Webster (diminutive of ceda, zeda, the letter z) and Wiktionary agree. The Visigothic-z story of the mark's shape is disputed, so the item says nothing about the shape's origin. rivalTest: argued for grave (the commonest confusion; it slopes down to the right, café's slopes up), circumflex (a hat shape, as in 'crêpe') and umlaut (two dots); none fits. 'Café' in English and French is always written with the acute when the accent is kept. volatility: evergreen. regional: café is written this way across the English-speaking world and in French, Spanish and Portuguese; the accent names are school knowledge in many countries. style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, explanation 27 words. myths: no match in myths.json. mystery and encore: not applicable to a practice item. doubts: none. Checked against every Daily item with content:dedupe.

evidence.restatement: Café is written with é, the e carrying a stroke that rises to the right: the acute.

claimResults.note: Solved cold. The word is borrowed from French café, whose é is the textbook example of the acute accent. Labelled high-risk only for the quoted word; nothing about it is uncertain or variable, so I confirm at certain confidence and rely on memo 18 for the second direct confirmation.

evidence.restatement: A grave falls to the right (è), a circumflex is a small roof (ê) and an umlaut is two dots (ë); the e of café shows none of these.

claimResults.note: Each distractor is a real diacritic of the same kind, so all three are plausible, and each is visibly a different shape from the mark in café. No reading makes any of them right.

evidence.restatement: The grave leans down from left to right, the mirror image of the acute, and the French preposition à in the phrase à la carte bears it.

claimResults.note: Both halves are basic French orthography: à (preposition) always takes the grave, distinguishing it from a (has).

evidence.restatement: In façade the c has a small hook beneath it, the cedilla, which marks a soft s sound before a.

claimResults.note: Standard French spelling, also kept in English in the form façade (often dropped as facade, which does not affect the claim).

evidence.restatement: Cedilla is a Spanish diminutive built on ceda or zeda, the old name of the letter z, because the mark began as a small z written under the c.

claimResults.note: This is the etymology given by the standard dictionaries (Spanish cedilla / zedilla, diminutive of ceda 'z'), and it matches the palaeographic history of the mark as a reduced subscript z in Visigothic script. High-risk etymology, held at certain confidence; under memo 18 it needs pass B's direct confirmation too. 'From Spanish for little z' in the explanation is a fair compression. No search spent given the cap of 2.

evidence.restatement: In the spelling café the e carries a stroke rising to the right, which is the acute accent (accent aigu).

claimResults.note: Rival test: the French word is fixed as café with an acute; the Spanish and Portuguese cafe variants are also acute. No variant with a grave or diaeresis exists. High risk only by C26's quotation floor; check A carries external evidence.

evidence.restatement: Café has neither a downward-left grave, a hat-shaped circumflex nor a two-dot umlaut or diaeresis over the e.

claimResults.note: Argued for umlaut (a learner might see a diacritic as an umlaut): wrong, as an umlaut is two dots. Grave versus acute is the only real confusion and it is settled by the direction of the stroke.

evidence.restatement: The grave accent leans the other way from the acute, and the à in à la carte carries one.

claimResults.note: Phrase is written à la carte in English and French dictionaries.

evidence.restatement: The little hook beneath the c in façade is called a cedilla.
Cedilla is a Spanish diminutive of zeda, the name of the letter z, so it means little z; the mark was a small z written under c.

claimResults.note: Etymology is high risk by rule; I am certain, and check A should supply external evidence.

issues.note: Fair everywhere: café is printed on signs worldwide, and the names of accents are taught in many school systems. Players who never learned accent names face a guess between acute and grave, which is the intended difficulty.

stem: What is the name of the mark above the letter e in the word 'café'?
